analysis.one_liner: Barred the Labor Department from writing rules that take overtime pay away from workers who currently have it.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee without ever getting a vote, leaving the Labor Department free to rewrite the overtime rules.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written the existing overtime rules into the Fair Labor Standards Act and told the Secretary of Labor: you cannot use regulation to put any additional worker into an exemption from overtime pay. The Department could still act in the other direction — extending overtime coverage to more workers — but could never shrink it. This was a direct response to the Labor Department's effort under the Bush administration to rewrite the white-collar exemption rules in ways that could strip overtime eligibility from millions of salaried workers. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, roughly the workers then covered by overtime rules — salaried employees near the exemption thresholds in fields like retail management, financial services, and health care — would have kept a statutory guarantee that no future regulation could take their overtime pay away. Workers who put in long hours would have kept the right to time-and-a-half past 40 hours a week even as the Department rewrote the definitions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Salaried workers at risk of losing overtime

how_it_helps.text: It barred the Secretary of Labor from issuing any rule that would exempt additional employees from overtime pay beyond those already exempt under the rules in effect when the bill became law.
It preserved the Department's ability to go the other way — the Secretary could still write rules that extend overtime protection to more workers.

analysis.who_pays: Employers whose business models rely on classifying large numbers of salaried employees as exempt from overtime would have borne the cost: any expansion of exemptions would have been off the table, keeping more employees eligible for time-and-a-half pay past 40 hours a week.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers relying on exempt salaried staff

drawbacks.text: The bill locked the existing exemption rules into statute as of the date of enactment, which would prevent the Labor Department from modernizing or clarifying the white-collar exemption rules in any direction that removed anyone from overtime coverage — even if an update were otherwise justified.

By hard-coding the 2003-era regulations, the bill left in place longstanding ambiguities in the white-collar exemptions that were a recurring source of wage litigation, rather than allowing the Department to rewrite those definitions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was large and concrete: keeping overtime pay available to the workers who had it, at a moment when the executive branch was rewriting the rules in the other direction. The cost was flexibility — the bill wrote the existing exemptions into statute, so even a well-designed future update would have needed Congress to act. On balance the bill traded a modest loss of regulatory flexibility for protection against a broad loss of overtime pay, and the committee system never let that trade reach a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced and never came out, so it never reached the Senate floor for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 29, 2003, read twice, and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005.
Twenty Democratic senators cosponsored the bill alongside Kennedy, yet it still never received committee or floor consideration.

The bill would have stopped the Labor Department from using regulation to add employees to the FLSA's overtime exemptions, a rewrite the Bush administration's Labor Department was pursuing at the time.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers came out ahead: with the bill dead, the Labor Department was left free to finalize its own rewrite of the overtime rules without the statutory limit Kennedy proposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, whose overtime liability stayed limited

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to lock in existing overtime protections and referred it to the HELP Committee.

for.name: 20 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Harkin, Schumer, Leahy, Durbin, Reid, Dodd, Stabenow, Mikulski, and Clinton.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: His administration's Labor Department proposed the rewrite of the overtime exemption rules the bill was designed to block, and he threatened to veto legislation that restricted the new rules.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the remaining year and a half of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill or a similar overtime-protection measure for Senate floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the committee that buried the bill was chaired by a Republican in a Republican-led Senate; no Republican supported the bill at any stage in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have kept overtime-pay liability off the table for employers by barring rules that reclassify more salaried workers as exempt. It died, so employers were freed to benefit from the Labor Department's rewrite instead.

industries.industry: Retail, financial services, and other large hourly-and-salaried workforces
industries.note: Sectors with large numbers of workers near the exemption salary threshold had the most to gain from the Department's proposed exemptions, which the bill would have blocked. Because the bill never got a vote, those sectors kept the wider exemption the rewrite allowed.
